title: Party-list: Legislation is the solution (2)
primary_topics: How party-list winners are determined -- the Veterans formula (Panganiban formula) and the Banat modification
The mathematical inscrutability and contradictions of RA 7941 as the root cause of recurring party-list controversies
CJ call for Congress to redefine, reengineer, or repeal the party-list system via legislation
sub_topics: Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec (Oct. 6, 2000) -- first SC ruling on party-list winners; the Veterans/Panganiban formula
RA 7941 four parameters: (1) 20% allocation, (2) 2% threshold, (3) 3-seat limit, (4) proportional representation
Veterans formula criticized: allegedly violated proportional representation; did not result in a rough straight line when graphed
Formula merely reflected RA 7941 parameters -- precise proportional representation requires amending the law
Veterans affirmed unanimously: Partido ng Manggagawa v. Comelec (March 15, 2006); Cibac v. Comelec (April 13, 2007)
Banat v. Comelec (April 21, 2009): declared 2% threshold unconstitutional; authorized seats for groups with less than 2% of votes
Banat distortions: topnotchers still limited to 3 seats; parties with less than 1% can win; Veterans allowed 14 party-list reps, Banat authorized 55
SC does not make, amend or invent laws -- only declares them valid or invalid
Congress options: (1) define PH party-list system clearly; (2) declare whether reserved for marginalized or open to all; (3) reengineer winner-determination method; OR (4) repeal RA 7941 altogether

stances.claim: RA 7941 is vague, contradictory and mathematically inscrutable -- its four parameters cannot all be satisfied simultaneously, making any judicial formula including the Panganiban formula necessarily imperfect.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-critical-yet-justified defense of own formula (the law is the problem, not the formula)

stances.claim: Banat modification -- voiding the 2% threshold while retaining the 3-seat cap -- produced worse distortions than Veterans: parties with less than 1% of votes can now win, topnotchers still limited to 3 seats, and 55 reps entered instead of 14.

The real and only lasting solution is congressional legislation: Congress must either clearly define and reengineer the party-list system or repeal RA 7941 -- leaving RA 7941 as is will continue to confound everyone.

notable_anecdotes: CJ identifying himself as the ponente of Veterans -- Panganiban formula because I was the ponente -- disclosing personal authorship before defending the formula while attributing its flaws to RA 7941 own contradictions.
The German parliamentary system as the origin of the party-list concept, mongrelized into the Philippine presidential system -- the most evocative word in the column for the structural mismatch.

Banat extreme outcome: a party with less than 1% of total votes cast can now win a party-list seat -- the single most absurd concrete consequence of voiding the 2% threshold while retaining the 3-seat cap.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban takes up the second major party-list question -- how winners are determined -- tracing the evolution from Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec (October 6, 2000), where he was the ponente of what became known as the 'Veterans/Panganiban formula,' through Banat v. Comelec (April 21, 2009). The root problem is RA 7941 itself, which is 'vague, contradictory and mathematically inscrutable': its four parameters -- 20% allocation, 2% threshold, 3-seat limit, and proportional representation -- are internally contradictory and cannot be satisfied simultaneously, making any judicial formula imperfect. The Veterans formula was unanimously affirmed in Partido ng Manggagawa (2006) and Cibac (2007), but Banat modified it by declaring the 2% threshold unconstitutional -- producing worse distortions: groups with less than 1% of votes can now win, poll topnotchers are still capped at 3 seats, and 55 party-list representatives entered the House instead of 14. Since the SC can only declare laws valid or invalid (not make or amend laws), the only lasting solution is congressional action: either clearly define and reengineer the PH party-list system, or repeal RA 7941 altogether. CJ closes dryly: leaving RA 7941 as is will 'continue to confound and confuse everyone, including its own honorable members. And the people.'
